record.original_question: What is the physical nature of the dark energy that supplies about three-fourths of the critical energy density, does not cluster like matter, and drives the observed accelerated expansion of the Universe?

evidence.quote: At the same time, the estimates of the energy density related to matter contribute ∼ 0.25ρc, that is the remaining three fourths of the energy density of the Universe are due to something else.

This contribution, whose primary difference form the matter contribution is in the absence of clustering (that is of concentration in stars, galaxies, clusters etc.), carries a not fully successful name of “dark energy”.
The question about the nature of the dark energy is presently open.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In the standard cosmological framework, the spatially flat Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker metric describes a homogeneous and isotropic Universe whose scale factor a(t) evolves according to the Friedmann equation H^2 = (8πG/3) ρ_total, where H = ȧ/a is the Hubble parameter and ρ_total is the total energy density. The critical density is ρ_c = 3H_0^2 / (8πG), with H_0 the present Hubble constant. Observations (including Type Ia supernovae luminosity distances, cosmic microwave background anisotropies, baryon acoustic oscillations, and large-scale structure) indicate that:

1. The total energy density of the Universe is approximately equal to ρ_c.
2. The contribution from matter (baryonic plus cold dark matter) is approximately 0.25 ρ_c, while the remaining ≈ 0.75 ρ_c is supplied by an unknown component conventionally called "dark energy".
3. Unlike matter, this component does not cluster gravitationally on the scales of galaxies and clusters: its energy density remains nearly spatially uniform.
4. Its effective equation of state w = p/ρ satisfies w ≈ −1 (with current bounds close to w = −1), so that this component drives an accelerated expansion ä > 0 of the Universe at late times.

Determine the physical nature of this dark-energy component. In particular, identify whether it corresponds to a true cosmological constant Λ (constant vacuum energy density), to a dynamical scalar field (e.g., quintessence, k-essence, phantom field) with time- and possibly space-dependent equation of state w(t), to a modification of general relativity on cosmological scales, or to some other mechanism, and derive a fundamental theoretical description that quantitatively reproduces the observed value Ω_DE ≈ 0.75, the observed equation of state w ≈ −1, and the absence of clustering on sub-horizon scales.
artifact.status_search_result: The nature of dark energy remains an open problem in fundamental physics and cosmology as of 2026. Recent results from DESI and other surveys hint at possible deviations from a pure cosmological constant (evolving w), but no consensus theoretical explanation has been established.

status_evidence.title: DESI 2024 cosmology results
status_evidence.snippet: DESI's first year results suggest dark energy may be evolving over time, challenging the cosmological constant interpretation, but the nature of dark energy remains unknown.
status_evidence.claim: Dark energy's fundamental nature is still unresolved; recent data hints at dynamical behavior.

status_evidence.title: Dark energy review (Annual Reviews)
status_evidence.snippet: The physical origin of cosmic acceleration—whether a cosmological constant, dynamical field, or modified gravity—remains an open question.
status_evidence.claim: Open status of the dark-energy nature question is reaffirmed in standard reviews.
